title: The God Who Is Not Nice
subtitle: Recovering the Holy God a Therapeutic Church Traded Away
blurb: The functioning god of much of the American church is warm, agreeable, and reliably on our side, and he cannot save anyone. James Bell, who came to faith from a settled atheism and did not leave unbelief for a god that small, traces the sentimental deity to his birth records, the five-article creed Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton named in 2005 and the therapeutic turn Philip Rieff saw coming in 1966, and then walks the reader back into the text, to the burning bush, the shaking doorposts of Isaiah 6, the terrified boat on Galilee, and Bonhoeffer's war on cheap grace. Written by a pastor who preached the nice god because it filled rooms, and stopped. The holy God is not safe. He was never nice. He is good, and he is the only comfort that holds.

chapters.title: The God We Would Prefer
chapters.summary: Bell lays out the thesis from inside his own failure. The church has traded the holy God of the Bible for a sentimental one who exists to affirm and console, and the trade is not maturity but idolatry made of nice materials. Neither the mean god nor the nice god is the God who is, and a former atheist explains why only the holy one was ever believable.
chapters.body:
I need to tell you something about myself before I tell you anything about God, because the two are more tangled than I would like them to be. The God I preach on Sunday is not always the God I want on Tuesday. The God I want on Tuesday is smaller. He is more agreeable. He fits in the palm of my afternoon and does not ask me to rearrange my life around him. He affirms the decisions I have already made. He is proud of me for reasons I have not earned. He is, in a word that has quietly become the highest compliment my culture can pay to anyone or anything, nice.

I came to faith late, and I came to it from the outside. I was an atheist not as a pose but as a settled conviction, a man who had done the reading and reached what he believed was the honest conclusion. When I finally could not hold that ground any longer, when the God I had denied turned out to be real in a way that undid me, I did not meet a nice God. That is the first thing I want you to know. The God who broke into my unbelief was not warm the way a blanket is warm. He was terrible the way a sunrise is terrible if you have spent your whole life underground. He was not comfortable. He was true, and the truth of him rearranged everything, and there was a period of weeks when I could not sleep because I had spent my adult life being confidently wrong about the most important thing there is. That God did not affirm me. That God saved me, which is a different and heavier act.

And yet within a year of my conversion I had started to sand him down. I did it without deciding to. It happens the way water finds the low place. I began to prefer the parts of God that consoled me and to grow quiet about the parts that unsettled me. I built, in the privacy of my own devotional life, a God who was mostly agreeable, occasionally sad about the state of the world, and reliably on my side. I preached the big God on Sunday and lived with the small one the rest of the week. I suspect you have done the same thing, though your version has different features than mine. We are, all of us, in the business of God management, and business is good.

So let me state the thesis of this book plainly, right here, so you can decide whether you want to keep reading. We have exchanged the holy, weighty, dangerous God of the Bible for a sentimental one who exists to affirm us and keep us comfortable. We have made a God who is nice. And nice is not holy. Nice is a small, thin, domesticated thing, a virtue for dinner parties, and we have draped it over the Ancient of Days and told ourselves we were being loving. We were not being loving. We were being cowardly, and we were being bored, and we were, though we would never say it this way, trying to make God safe.

Let me also be precise about what I am not saying, because the false alternative will kill this book in your hands if I do not kill it first. I am not arguing for a mean God. That is the trap everyone falls into the moment you criticize the sentimental one. They assume that if you take away the nice God you must be reaching for the cruel one, the angry deity of the worst sermons any of us have sat through, the God who is basically disappointed in you and looking for a reason to strike. That God is a heresy too. He is the sentimental God's evil twin, just as false, just as much a projection of the human heart, only this time the fearful, self-hating part of it. I am not offering you that God. I am asking you to consider that the true God is neither nice nor mean, because both of those words belong to the world of the small and the manageable. The true God is holy. And holiness is a category we have almost entirely lost the ability to feel.

Rudolf Otto, writing in 1917 in a book called The Idea of the Holy, reached for a word that did not exist because the thing he was describing had fallen out of Christian speech. He called it the numinous. He said that when human beings encounter the holy they encounter a mysterium tremendum et fascinans, a mystery that makes you tremble and that draws you in at the same time, a reality so far above you that it overwhelms your capacity to hold it and yet so compelling that you cannot look away. That is the God of the burning bush, the God who tells Moses to take off his shoes because the ground itself has become dangerous with holiness. That is the God who fills the temple with smoke until Isaiah is undone. We do not have a category for that anymore. We have replaced tremendum with pleasant. We have taken the God who made Moses hide his face and turned him into a God who is glad you came to church and hopes you have a nice week.

Now let me describe the God I would build if the building were left to me, because I suspect you have built one very like him, and it will help us both to see him in daylight, laid out on the table where we can look at what our hands have made. My God, the one I construct when no one is watching and I am not being careful, is warm. He is endlessly warm. He has the emotional temperature of a good counselor who also happens to like me personally. He is interested in my flourishing, and he defines my flourishing in terms I would have chosen anyway. He is not, if I am honest, terribly interested in my sin, because my sin embarrasses him a little the way it embarrasses me, and we have a tacit agreement not to bring it up. He is proud of me. He affirms my choices. And above every other quality, he is comfortable to be around. I never leave his presence shaken. I never leave undone. I leave, if anything, a little more pleased with myself than when I arrived.

That God is an idol, and I made him, and I keep making him, and the fact that I made him out of nice materials instead of gold does not make him any less of an idol. An idol is not necessarily an ugly thing. The golden calf was beautiful. The idols of the ancient world were often the finest artistic achievements of their cultures. An idol is simply a god of our own construction, a deity shaped to our specifications, a divinity we can predict and manage and, when necessary, put back on the shelf. By that definition the nice God is the most successful idol the modern West has ever produced, precisely because he does not look like an idol. He looks like kindness. He looks like the mature, non-judgmental, inclusive faith we flatter ourselves for having achieved. But strip away the flattering language and you find the oldest sin there is, the sin of making God in our own image, of reaching up into heaven and pulling God down to a size we can carry in one hand.

A.W. Tozer saw this coming. In 1961, in The Knowledge of the Holy, he argued that what comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us, and that a low view of God is the cause of a hundred lesser evils in the soul before it ever becomes visible in the life. He was not warning about atheism. He was warning about shrinkage, about a church that would keep every word of its vocabulary and lose the weight behind the words. Take the name off that sentence and it still stands on its own evidence, which is why I keep his name on it. He described, four decades early, exactly the church I have spent fifteen years pastoring.

And here I can offer you something the lifelong churchgoer cannot, because I spent my adult years on the other side of the argument. The nice God is not merely false. He is unbelievable. No honest atheist was ever kept awake by him. If someone had offered me, in my unbelieving years, a deity whose function was to affirm my choices and want my happiness, I would have recognized him instantly as a product, something manufactured to meet a demand, and I would have been right. A god who never contradicts you is indistinguishable from your own reflection, and I already had one of those. The God who eventually broke me was believable for precisely the reasons he was unwelcome. He kept refusing to be what I wanted. He had edges I did not put there. I did not leave a serious unbelief for a small god. Nobody does. People do not abandon their honest conclusions for a scented candle.

So here is where we are going. I am going to walk you back into the throne room. I am going to show you where the nice God came from, because he has a history and a birth certificate, and then I am going to take you to the burning bush and to Sinai and to the temple where the doorposts shook, and I am going to stand you in the boat with twelve terrified men who discovered that the storm was the second most frightening thing on the water that night. I am going to keep confessing, all the way through, that I am the man who prefers the small God. I am not writing this from above you. Every argument in this book is an argument I have had to have with myself, usually more than once, usually losing the early rounds. What I have found, and what I am asking you to find with me, is that every time I have let the small God die, the great God has proven to be the only one who could carry the weight I actually brought him. We ran from the weight of God because we thought it would crush us. It is the only thing that can hold us up.

You picked the kinder lie. I did too. Let us go and find the harder truth, and see if it is not, in the end, the only thing gentle enough to save us.
chapters.verdict: We made him small because small is safe.
reflect: Describe the God you actually pray to on an ordinary Tuesday. How closely does he resemble the God you would design if the design were up to you?
Bell says the opposite of the nice god is not a mean god but a holy one. Where have you seen those two categories collapsed into each other?
If you do not believe in God, consider the god most often presented to you by modern churches. Would a God with edges you could not have invented be more or less credible to you?
What would you lose, honestly, if the God who affirms your choices turned out not to exist?

chapters.title: The Creed Nobody Wrote Down
chapters.summary: In 2005 Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton named the actual functioning religion of American young people, Moralistic Therapeutic Deism, a five-article creed with no sin, no cross, and no cost. The teenagers did not invent it. They inherited it from us, and Bell runs the audit on his own pulpit and finds the parasite fed there too.
chapters.body:
If you want to know what a church actually believes, do not read its statement of faith. Ask its teenagers. They have not yet learned which parts of the family religion are said out loud and which parts are quietly retired, so they will tell you, with the devastating candor of the young, what they actually absorbed at our tables and in our pews. For years I would ask students in my own church what they believed about God, and I would get answers that were warm, kind, vague, and interchangeable with what any pleasant unbelieving neighbor might say. God exists. God wants us to be good people. God wants me to be happy. I did not think much of it at the time. I thought it was a phase, something depth would come along and fix. I was wrong about that, and the proof arrived in 2005 with footnotes attached.

That year the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton published Soul Searching, the report of the National Study of Youth and Religion, the most comprehensive study of the religious lives of American teenagers that had ever been conducted. They surveyed thousands of young people across the country and sat with hundreds of them for long personal interviews, and what they found was not rebellion and it was not atheism. American teenagers were not rejecting religion. They were practicing one, a real and coherent one, with actual doctrines, and it had simply never been written down. Smith and Denton wrote it down. They gave it a name that has haunted the American church ever since. They called it Moralistic Therapeutic Deism.

Its creed, as they reconstructed it from the mouths of the young, has five articles. First, a God exists who created the world and watches over human life. Second, God wants people to be good, nice, and fair to each other, which is what the Bible and most religions teach. Third, the central goal of life is to be happy and to feel good about oneself. Fourth, God does not need to be particularly involved in your life except when you have a problem he is needed to solve. Fifth, good people go to heaven when they die.

Read those five articles twice. The first time you will notice what is there, and it will seem harmless, even sweet. The second time you will notice what is missing, and the list of what is missing is the entire Christian faith. There is no sin in that creed. There is no cross. There is no repentance, no judgment, no holiness, no resurrection, no covenant, no worship, no cost. There is a God who watches from a distance, approves of niceness, sponsors your self-esteem, waits by the phone in case of emergency, and admits the well-behaved to heaven on the strength of their record. It is not a rough draft of Christianity. It is a different religion that has learned to wear Christian clothes, and it fits so comfortably that most of its adherents will live and die inside our churches without ever noticing they belong to something else.

Smith and Denton described the God of this creed in an image I have never been able to shake. He functions, they observed, as something like a divine butler crossed with a cosmic therapist, a being who is professionally available, who answers when rung for, who helps his clients feel better about themselves and resolve their problems, and who otherwise keeps a discreet distance from their affairs. And they made a second observation that matters even more. Moralistic Therapeutic Deism, they argued, does not build its own institutions. It has no seminaries and plants no congregations. It is parasitic. It colonizes existing faiths from the inside, feeding on their language and their buildings and their budgets while quietly replacing their content, so that a church can preach Christ crucified in its documents and Moralistic Therapeutic Deism from its actual pulpit and never feel the seam.

But the finding that should keep pastors and parents awake is the one the headlines skipped. The teenagers did not invent this religion. Teenagers do not invent religions. They inherit them. Smith and Denton were clear that the young people in their study were faithfully mirroring the actual functioning faith of their parents and their congregations, reflecting back not what the adults professed but what the adults practiced and prized. The kids were not the corruption. The kids were the audit. They said loudly and artlessly what we had been saying quietly and artfully for a generation, and when we recoiled from their five-point creed we were recoiling from our own reflection with the flattery removed.

I know this because I ran the audit on myself, and I am going to tell you what I found, because this book has no right to point at American Christianity in general if it will not point at the pulpit of First Baptist Church of Fenton in particular. Some years ago I sat down with a stack of my own sermon manuscripts and asked one question of each. If a committed Moralistic Therapeutic Deist had heard this sermon, at what point would he have squirmed. At what point would his creed and my preaching have come into open conflict. There were sermons, more than I want to admit, where the honest answer was never. Sermons where God existed, wanted us to be good, wanted us to be happy, was available for our problems, and was never once holy. Sermons a butler could have taken no offense at. I preached them, people thanked me at the door, and the parasite fed.

Now I want to be fair to this creed, because it is not stupid, and the people who hold it are not fools, and a verdict that has not passed through fairness is just a mood. Every one of the five articles is a corruption of something true. God does watch over the world. He does want goodness, and the Bible does command fairness and kindness. Joy really is promised to the people of God, and Scripture is not embarrassed by happiness. God really does invite us to bring him our problems, and cast your anxieties on him is a verse, not a slogan. Heaven is real. Moralistic Therapeutic Deism is not a pack of lies. It is a set of truths with the tension removed, Christianity with everything that costs anything carefully deleted, each doctrine kept exactly up to the point where it would make a demand and then filed smooth. That is why it survives so well in churches. Every sentence of it can be defended with a verse, so long as nobody reads the next verse.

The fourth article is the tell. A God who does not need to be involved in your life except when you have a problem is not the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He is not even a pagan god, because the pagan gods at least demanded things. He is a smoke detector. He hangs quietly on the ceiling of your life, required by code, ignored by design, and if he ever goes off during dinner you stand on a chair and take the battery out. The deism in Moralistic Therapeutic Deism is the polite word for this arrangement. The old deists at least had the honesty to say their god had wound the clock and walked away. We have improved on them. Our god stays close enough to be useful and far enough to be no trouble, which is to say we have designed a god around our own convenience, and convenience is the one thing the God of the Bible has never once been.

You can measure what this religion produces by listening to its people try to speak. Smith and Denton found that the teenagers they interviewed, including the churchgoing ones, were strikingly inarticulate about their faith, able to talk fluently about their classes and their friendships and their plans, and reduced to shrugs and fragments when asked about God. The researchers noted that these same students could hold forth on any subject that had actually been taught to them. The inarticulacy was the evidence. You cannot speak at length about something that has no weight in your life, and you cannot testify to a God whose entire function is to agree with you. There is nothing to say about the nice god. He has no history, no demands, no danger, and no story, and the silence of two generations of church kids is the sound of that emptiness being politely inherited.

And it was inherited from further back than their parents. The creed nobody wrote down has been getting written for a long time. You can hear it forming in the sentimental hymnody of the nineteenth century, which began trading the majesty of God for the coziness of Jesus as personal companion. You can watch it organize itself in the revivalism that learned to treat conversion as a product and the audience as a market, and in the positive-thinking empire of the twentieth century, where Norman Vincent Peale sold The Power of Positive Thinking in 1952 to a nation that wanted its religion to work like a tonic. None of those movements meant to found a new religion. Each of them just moved the center of gravity one inch toward the self, and an inch a generation is all it takes. By the time the sociologists arrived with their clipboards, the God of Sinai had become the God of self-esteem, and no council had ever voted on it, and no one had ever repented of it, because no one had ever noticed it.

That is the real terror of Soul Searching, and it is why I have spent a whole chapter on a twenty-year-old study instead of nodding at it in passing. Heresy used to announce itself. Arius had a position and defended it, and the church could gather at Nicaea in 325 and answer him. But nobody defends Moralistic Therapeutic Deism, because nobody knows they hold it. It is not a position. It is a sediment. It settles silently, over decades, in hymnals and youth curricula and pastoral habits and the ten thousand small decisions about what will preach, until one day the sociologists interview your children and hand you back a creed you never wrote and cannot deny. We get the god we actually teach, not the one we profess. I have five sons. They will not inherit the God of my statement of faith. They will inherit the God of my Tuesday nights, the one I actually trust or fail to trust when the bill comes or the diagnosis lands, and no orthodoxy on paper will protect them from what I really worship. The creed nobody wrote down is written somewhere. It is written on us.
chapters.verdict: We taught them the creed. They believed us.
reflect: Read the five articles of Moralistic Therapeutic Deism slowly. Which one is hardest for you to distinguish from your own working faith?
Bell calls the creed truths with the tension removed. Pick one article and name both the truth inside it and the cost that was deleted from it.
If the young people of a church are the audit of what it actually teaches, what would the teenagers you know report about your community?
What does the inarticulacy of churchgoing teenagers about their own faith suggest about the weight of what they were given?

chapters.title: The Triumph of the Therapeutic
chapters.summary: Why did we build the nice god? Bell takes the wound seriously first, the cruel churches and the real discoveries of psychology, then turns to Philip Rieff, who saw in 1966 that faith would survive the therapeutic age by converting itself into a supplier of well-being. The verdict is the standing one. The therapeutic got the symptom right and the anthropology wrong.
chapters.body:
Why did we build him. If the last chapter is right, if the functioning religion of much of the American church is a warm deism with a therapist's bedside manner, then the question deserves a real answer and not a sneer, because nobody trades the God of Sinai for a smoke detector out of simple wickedness. Something happened to us. Something made the trade feel not like a betrayal but like a mercy, and until we name that something honestly, every criticism in this book is just a man yelling at people whose wounds he has not bothered to examine.

So let me examine the wounds, and let me do it at full strength, because they are real. A great many people were handed the mean God first. They were raised under the angry deity of the worst kind of church, the God who was always disappointed, always watching for the failure, always ready with the belt. They were children when they learned that God was mostly displeased with them, and some of them learned it from pulpits and some of them learned it from fathers, and the two teachers often worked in shifts. And the church did not merely teach a cruel God. It behaved like one. It shamed grief as weak faith. It told the depressed to pray harder and treated their medication as a confession of unbelief. It counseled women to endure what no one should be counseled to endure. It protected the reputations of institutions over the bodies of children, and when the wounded finally spoke, it questioned their motives. I am a pastor. These are my people and my profession, and I will not pretend the prosecution has no case. The case is strong, and parts of it are unanswerable.

Into that wounded world came the therapeutic revolution, and it found things that were actually there. Trauma is real, and it does not leave when you rebuke it. Anxiety is real, a body-deep alarm that does not switch off for a sermon. The clinicians and researchers of the last century mapped territories of human suffering that the church had been content to moralize about, and they built instruments that genuinely help, and I say that without hedging because I have watched counseling hold marriages and lives together in my own congregation, including lives the church's own cruelty had helped break. When psychology offered the wounded a language for their pain that did not begin by blaming them for it, they took the language. They were not wrong to take it. If the church loses a generation to therapy, the first question is not what is wrong with therapy. It is what the church was doing that made a stranger's office feel safer than the household of God.

That is the steelman, and I want it standing in full view while I now tell you what happened next, because what happened next is that the medicine became a religion. The man who saw it coming was not a preacher. Philip Rieff was a sociologist, and in 1966 he published The Triumph of the Therapeutic, a book about what happens to a civilization when it changes its mind about what a human being is for. Every culture before ours, Rieff argued, functioned as a system of shared commitments. A culture worked by binding people to purposes beyond themselves, by teaching renunciation, by telling its members what they must give up and whom they must serve, and its ideal figures were the saint, the sage, the citizen, the believer. What Rieff saw arriving was the first culture in history organized around the opposite principle, around release rather than commitment, and its ideal figure was new. Religious man was born to be saved, he wrote, and psychological man is born to be pleased. The old question was, how can I be righteous. The new question was, how do I feel.

Rieff's sharpest insight, and the one this book turns on, was his prediction about what would happen to faith. The churches, he saw, would mostly not be closed. They would be converted. Religious institutions would survive the therapeutic age by quietly changing function, retaining their buildings and their vocabularies while becoming suppliers of the one commodity the new culture demanded, a manageable sense of well-being. The congregation would remain a congregation in form and become a clientele in fact. Faith would no longer bind. It would soothe. And a faith whose job is to soothe cannot ever afford to say a hard thing, which means it cannot afford holiness, which means the God of Sinai had to go, not because anyone disproved him but because he was bad for the customer experience. Rieff published that argument the year my parents' generation was young. He was not describing a fringe. He was describing, in advance, the mainstream of American religion, the world Smith and Denton would find fully built four decades later.

Charles Taylor gave us the other half of the diagnosis. In A Secular Age, published in 2007, he described the modern person as a buffered self, insulated by a kind of protective shell against the transcendent. The ancient person lived porous, open to a world thick with God and spirits and meanings that arrived from outside and could not be controlled. The modern person lives defended, with the self at the center and the transcendent waiting outside the shell, admitted by appointment only, and mostly the appointment is never made. The nice god is the god of the buffered self. He has agreed to the terms. He stays outside until summoned, respects the boundary, never overwhelms. A God who cannot overwhelm you cannot save you either, but that is the price of the buffer, and we have mostly decided the safety is worth it.

Now measure the therapeutic age by its own promise. The promise was that if we organized everything around the well-being of the self, the self would finally be well. We have had two full generations of the experiment. The self has never been more attended to, more analyzed, more affirmed, more curated, more medicated, more relentlessly the center of every institution it touches, including the church. And by the reckoning of the researchers themselves, the self is not well. Jonathan Haidt, in The Anxious Generation in 2024, documented the collapse into anxiety and fragility of precisely the young people raised most completely inside the culture of self-focus, and whatever weight you give his particular causes, the broad finding is not in dispute. The most therapeutic culture in history is among the most anxious cultures in history. That correlation does not prove the therapy caused the anxiety. It does prove the therapy has not cured it, and after sixty years of triumph, the burden of proof has changed sides.

Here is the verdict I think the evidence requires, and it is the standing verdict of this whole platform when Scripture reads the social sciences. The therapeutic got the symptom right and the anthropology wrong. It saw truly that people are wounded, anxious, and carrying weight they did not choose, and the church should have the humility to say that the clinicians often saw it first and described it better. But it misread the creature. It assumed the deepest thing wrong with a human being is pain, and therefore the deepest need is relief. Scripture says the deepest thing wrong with a human being is a ruptured relationship with a holy God, and pain is downstream, and therefore the deepest need is not relief but reconciliation, and the self cannot supply it to itself. There is one sentence the therapeutic can never say, and it is the only sentence that finally heals. You are guilty, and you are loved, and the guilt has been dealt with at a cost you did not pay. Forgiveness is not in the inventory. It cannot be, because forgiveness requires a wronged party with the standing to forgive, and the buffered self allowed no one through the shell with that kind of authority.

I want to be precise here, because this chapter will be misread if I am not. This is not an argument against counseling. I send people from my own congregation to counselors, and I will keep doing it, and the good ones are honest about the limits of their office in a way that should shame many pulpits. A competent counselor will tell you plainly that she can help you understand your patterns and carry your grief, and that she cannot absolve you, because absolution is not hers to give. The target of this chapter is not the clinic. It is the church that converted itself into one. When the church becomes a clinic it becomes a bad clinic, offering neither the professional rigor of actual psychology nor the terrible medicine of actual grace, and the sign over its door still says the household of God, and the God in question would not recognize what is practiced there.

And before anyone on the political right enjoys this chapter too much, let me turn the same instrument around, because the therapeutic god has a brother, and the brother carries a flag. A god conscripted to soothe the self and a god conscripted to win for the tribe are the same idol in different uniforms. Both exist to serve their owners. Both are managed. Both can be relied upon never to turn and speak against the people who keep them. The congregation that wants only comfort and the congregation that wants only victory have both replaced the God who is with a god who is useful, and I have grieved in both kinds of rooms, and the grief is the same grief. This book fires at the therapeutic god because he is the one my era mass-produced. The nationalist god gets the same charge from the same instrument, and we will meet him again before we are done.

I will end where I have to end, which is closer to home. I am a therapeutic man. I was formed in this culture, not above it. I preach better than I pray. When I am exhausted I do not reach for the God of the whirlwind, I reach for the god who is pleased with me, and I know exactly which features to give him because I have been drawing them my whole believing life. The wound that built the nice god was real. The medicine that treated the wound was real. And then, somewhere while nobody was watching, the medicine became the religion, and we began to worship our own relief. That is the history. The wounded fled a cruel god, the culture handed them a kind one, and nobody asked whether kind and true were the same thing. They are not the same thing. It is time to go and meet what is true.
chapters.verdict: The wound was real. The medicine became the god.
reflect: Where has the church genuinely wounded you or someone you love, and what god did that wound tempt you to build in response?
Rieff said religious man was born to be saved and psychological man is born to be pleased. Which man wakes up in your body most mornings?
Bell argues the one sentence therapy cannot say is, you are guilty and you are loved. Why does that sentence require someone outside the self to say it?
How would you tell the difference between a church that cares for wounded people and a church that has quietly become a clinic?

chapters.title: Take Off Your Shoes
chapters.summary: Exodus 3 unfolded. The God of the burning bush teaches Moses distance before he gives him a mission, gives a name that refuses every handle, and then descends on Sinai in fire while announcing a rescue. The tremendum and the compassion are one speech, and our carpeted, fear-proofed worship rooms testify against the text every week.
chapters.body:
Now we go to the text, because everything so far has been diagnosis, and diagnosis can only tell you what you lost. The text is where we find out what we lost. And the text does not begin where our worship services begin, with reassurance. It begins in the wilderness on the far side of nowhere, with an eighty-year-old failure watching someone else's sheep.

That is what Moses is when Exodus 3 opens, and we should not rush past it. Forty years earlier he had been a prince of Egypt with a conscience, and the conscience had gotten a man killed, and the prince had run. Now he keeps the flock of his father-in-law in the land of Midian, which is the ancient world's way of saying he is nobody, employed by his in-laws, at an age when a man's story is over. He leads the flock to the west side of the wilderness and comes to Horeb, the mountain of God, though nothing in the text suggests he knows to call it that yet. To Moses it is a mountain. To Moses it is Tuesday.

Then a bush is on fire, which in a desert is not remarkable, except that this one keeps burning. The text is careful here in a way we are usually not. The angel of the LORD appears to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush, and Moses looks, and the bush is burning, yet it is not consumed. What draws him is not terror. It is curiosity. He says he will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned. And then comes a sentence I preached for years before I noticed it. When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush. God waits for the turning. The fire is lit first, and the man must turn aside from the path and the flock and the ordinary Tuesday, and only then does the voice come. There is a whole theology of attention in that verse. The bushes are burning all around us, and we have very good phones.

The voice calls his name twice, Moses, Moses, the doubled name that in Scripture always means love and always means gravity, and Moses answers the way the ready always answer, here I am. And what God says next is the hinge of this entire book. He does not say, relax, this is a safe place. He does not say, I am so glad you are here. He says, do not come near. He says, take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground. And then he introduces himself as the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.

Stay inside that moment and feel how strange it is. The dirt of Horeb is the same dirt it was the day before. Nothing about the ground has changed except its proximity to God, and proximity is enough. Holiness radiates. It makes ordinary things dangerous the way voltage makes ordinary wire dangerous, and the first lesson God teaches the man who will carry his name to a nation is not a doctrine and not a mission. It is a boundary. Take off your shoes. You are closer than you think to something you do not understand. Before Moses learns what God will do, he learns what God is, and what God is makes a man cover his face in the presence of a shrub.

But now watch the direction this holiness moves, because here is where the mean god and the nice god both lose the thread. The voice from the bush does not say, I have seen the affliction of my people and they had it coming. It says, I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them. The holy fire and the rescue mission are one speech. The God who will not let Moses come a step closer is the same God who has closed the distance between heaven and a slave camp because he could not bear the crying. This is Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans standing in front of us in narrative form, the God who makes you hide your face and the God you cannot look away from, terror and magnetism in a single flame. The mean god is all tremendum, dread with no rescue in it. The nice god is all approachability, warmth with no voltage in it. The God of the bush is both at once, and the both-at-once is the whole point, and it is exactly the thing we keep tearing in half.

Then Moses asks for the name. He asks practically, because he is already dreading the conversation in Egypt, and the people will ask who sent him, and names in the ancient world were not labels. They were handles. To know a god's name was to have a claim on him, a way to invoke him, something to grip. Every religion of the ancient Near East ran on this assumption, gods with names and appetites, gods you could feed and flatter and steer. And God answers Moses with the name that ends all handles. I AM WHO I AM. Say this to the people of Israel, I AM has sent me to you. It is a name that gives everything and concedes nothing. It promises presence, absolute, underived, unconditioned presence, and it refuses definition, because every definition is a wall around a thing and this one will not be walled. The LORD, as he will be called, the name English Bibles print in small capitals, is the God who will be known, deeply and covenantally known, and who will never once be managed. Israel will spend the rest of the Old Testament learning the difference, and the church has spent two thousand years trying to forget it.

Follow the story forward three chapters' worth of plagues and one dry seabed, and the freed slaves stand at the foot of the same mountain, because the God of the bush told Moses that this was the sign, you shall serve God on this mountain. Exodus 19 is what it looks like when the bush scales up. The mountain is wrapped in smoke because the LORD has descended on it in fire, the whole mountain trembles, there is thunder and lightning and a trumpet blast that grows louder and louder, and the people are commanded to set boundaries around the base and to touch nothing on pain of death. This is not stagecraft. It is the same lesson as the sandals, taught to a nation at once. Then God speaks the ten words, and the people cannot bear it. They tell Moses, you speak to us, and we will listen, but do not let God speak to us, lest we die. And Moses answers them with the sentence I will spend a later chapter unfolding, because it holds the whole paradox of the fear of God in fourteen words. Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin. Do not be afraid, and be afraid. Both, in one breath, from the man who knew this God face to face. Whatever that sentence means, it is not nice, and whatever it means, the people who heard it were changed by it, and we will come back for it.

Now set our Sunday mornings beside this text, mine included, and feel the distance. We have spent two generations engineering the fear out of the room. The lights are warm, the chairs are soft, the countdown clock relieves you of even the small terror of not knowing when things will start, and the opening line from the stage, in thousands of churches this week, will be some version of, relax, you belong here, this is a safe place. I understand every one of those choices. I have made most of them. Each one was hospitality, and hospitality is a Christian virtue, and the wounded people of chapter three needed a room that did not attack them. But somewhere in the accumulation of all that softness we crossed a line no one voted on, and the room built to welcome people began to testify, all by itself, that there is nothing here to tremble at. The medium became the message. The text says the ground near God is dangerous. Our architecture says the ground near God is carpeted. And a generation raised on the carpet does not believe us anymore when we read them the bush, because everything about the room says we do not believe it either.

Someone will say, and should say, that this is the Old Testament, that Sinai stands on the far side of the cross, that Hebrews itself declares we have not come to a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest. That objection deserves a whole chapter and it will get one, because what Hebrews actually says next is stranger and heavier than the objection thinks. But do not let the objection move too fast past what the bush already shows, which is that the fire and the mercy were never opposites even here, at maximum voltage, at the very first introduction. The bush burned and was not consumed. That is the gospel in its first appearance, presence that does not destroy what it fills, fire that a thing can live inside. Grace was never the reduction of the voltage. Grace was always the miracle that we survive it.

I did not understand Moses hiding his face until it happened to me. When the God I had spent my adult life denying finally cornered me, the sensation was not warmth and it was not welcome. It was exposure. It was the feeling of having been seen entirely, every rationalization lit at once, and my instinct was not to run toward it, it was to cover. I know now that the covering was the most honest thing I had done in years. A man who has actually stood near the fire does not have to be told to take off his shoes. He has to be told, later, tenderly, that he may come near again. Both sentences are in the text. We built a whole religion out of the second one and threw the first one away, and then wondered why the second one stopped meaning anything. The ground has not cooled. The fire is where it always was. We just stopped turning aside, and we kept our shoes on, and we called it progress.
chapters.verdict: The ground never cooled. We kept our shoes on.
reflect: God waited until Moses turned aside before he spoke. What in your life functions as the turning aside, and what is currently preventing it?
The name I AM WHO I AM promises presence and refuses management. Where do you catch yourself trying to use God rather than know him?
Bell says our worship spaces are engineered so that no one is ever afraid. What does the room you worship in teach, all by itself, about the God worshiped there?
The bush burned and was not consumed. What does it change to read that as the first appearance of grace rather than a special effect?

chapters.title: Undone
chapters.summary: Isaiah 6 unfolded. In the year King Uzziah died the best man in Jerusalem saw the thrice-holy God and came apart at the seams, and holiness found the sin in his best thing, not his worst. Then a coal from the altar, guilt named and atoned, and only afterward the sending. Holiness unmakes before it heals, and our discipleship runs the sequence backward.
chapters.body:
In the year that King Uzziah died. Isaiah dates his vision the way you date the things that reorganize you, by the public catastrophe they arrived inside, and the date matters. Uzziah had reigned in Judah for fifty-two years, longer than most lifetimes in the eighth century before Christ, a king so successful that his name had become another word for stability. When he died, around 740 BC, with the Assyrian empire sharpening itself to the north, an entire nation felt the floor move. Every living generation of Judah had known one king. Now the throne of Judah stood empty, and it was in that year, says Isaiah, that I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up. The earthly throne empties and the heavenly throne comes into view, occupied, as it always had been. Isaiah does not see God arrive. He sees what was there the whole time, once the furniture of his security is dragged out of the way. It is worth asking what furniture would have to be dragged out of your way, and it is worth remembering that God rarely asks.

What Isaiah sees, first, is scale. The Lord is sitting, not pacing, not reacting, enthroned, and the train of his robe filled the temple. Just the hem. The overflow of the garment of the overflow of the glory fills the largest sacred space Isaiah knows. And around the throne stand the seraphim, and here the text does something our sentimental angelology cannot survive. The word seraphim means burning ones. These are creatures of living flame who have never sinned, who have nothing to be ashamed of and nothing to fear, and each one has six wings, and four of the six are used for covering. With two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew. Sinless fire hides its face in that room. Creatures who have never once fallen do not presume on the sight of God. Whatever casualness with the Almighty we have taught ourselves, the seraphim have not heard of it.

And one called to another and said, Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts. Hebrew has no italics and no exclamation mark. When the language wants to intensify, it repeats, and when it wants a superlative, it repeats twice. A pit can be deep, or it can be deep, deep. Only one attribute of God is ever raised to the third power in all of Scripture. The Bible never says that God is love, love, love, though he is love, and it never says he is mercy, mercy, mercy, though his mercy is over all his works. It says holy, holy, holy, and it says it in both testaments, here and in Revelation 4, where the living creatures around the throne have not stopped saying it. Holiness is not one item on the list of God's qualities. It is the light in which every other quality burns, the Godness of God, his being in a category that contains only him. That is what the seraphim cannot stop announcing to each other, forever, as if it were always new information. And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. In our rooms, the subwoofer shakes the floor. In this room, the word holy does.

Now watch what this vision does to the man, because this is the verse on which the entire therapeutic gospel breaks. Isaiah is not a criminal dragged into the throne room. He is, by every earthly measure, the best man in Jerusalem, a prophet, an educated man, possibly a courtier, the kind of man any search committee in America would call without checking references. And his response to the unfiltered holiness of God is not inspiration. He says, woe is me, for I am lost, for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts. The Hebrew behind that word lost is nidmeti, and translators have circled it for centuries. Ruined. Undone. Unmade. It is the sound of a made thing coming apart at the seams. The old translators wrote, I am undone, and I have never found a better rendering, because what happens to Isaiah in that moment is precisely an un-doing, a coming apart of the assembled self, the reputation and the competence and the comparative righteousness all failing at once like stitching in a flood.

Notice where the unmaking finds him. Unclean lips. Not, I am a man of violent hands or wandering eyes. Lips. The prophet's instrument, the one part of himself he could be proudest of, his gift, his calling, his best thing. Holiness does not go looking for your worst thing. Your conscience already knows about your worst thing. Holiness finds the sin in your best thing, the vanity braided into the gift, the self buried in the service, and that is why the encounter is so devastating and so clarifying at once. Every comparative measure Isaiah owned, and he owned many, was calibrated against other men. One sight of the King recalibrated everything, and the best man in Jerusalem discovered that the difference between himself and the worst man in Jerusalem, so enormous at street level, does not survive the throne room.

If the vision ended there, we would have the mean god, dread with no rescue, and Isaiah would be right that he is lost. It does not end there. Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. Feel the detail. A creature made of fire uses tongs. Even the burning ones do not handle what has touched the altar of God with bare hands. And he touched my mouth, says Isaiah, the coal pressed to the exact place the confession named, and said, behold, this has touched your lips, your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for. Everything the nice god cannot say is in that sentence. Guilt, named as real. Atonement, accomplished, not negotiated. And everything the mean god cannot do is in the geometry of it, because the coal comes from the altar, the place of sacrifice, the place where something dies so that someone may live. Grace in this text is not the softening of holiness. Grace is holiness, on fire, applied directly to the wound, and it hurts, and it heals, in that order, and the order is not optional. The coal does not affirm Isaiah's lips. It cauterizes them.

Only then, and the order is everything, does the mission come. And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, whom shall I send, and who will go for us. Then I said, here I am. Send me. Undone, atoned, sent. That is the sequence, and it has never been repealed. The man who volunteers in verse eight is not the man who walked in at verse one. He is a man with nothing left to protect, which is the only kind of man God can send anywhere dangerous, because he has already died the death that mattered and found grace on the far side of it. Our discipleship pipeline mostly runs this sequence backward. We recruit on strengths, deploy on gifts, and hope character shows up in transit. We send people who have never been undone, and then we convene task forces to study why our leaders keep collapsing, and the answer is in the eighth century, in the smoke, on the record.

Rudolf Otto stood before this very chapter when he built his account of the holy, and what he saw in it he called creature-consciousness, the felt awareness of being dust and ashes in the presence of that which is not dust and not ashes. It is the same knowledge that meets Job in the whirlwind, where a suffering man demands a hearing and receives, instead of answers, the sight of God, and puts his hand over his mouth, and somehow finds that this is more than the answers would have been. The modern reader wants to protest that this is bad pastoral care. The record of the text is that it is the only pastoral care that has ever reached the bottom of a human being. Isaiah did not leave the temple with lower self-esteem. He left with no self-esteem in either direction, the whole exhausting apparatus of self-regard burned off his mouth with a coal, and what walked out was a free man.

I have stood, in my own small way, where he stood, and I told you the shape of it already, the weeks after my conversion when I could not sleep because I had been confidently wrong about everything that mattered. Nobody affirmed me into the kingdom of God. I was unmade into it. And I want to say this carefully, as a pastor and not a romantic. The unmaking is not the punishment. The unmaking is the mercy. The self I had assembled could not have carried what was coming into my life, the marriage, the five sons, the congregation, the deaths I would sit beside, and God in his severity did not repair that self. He replaced its foundation. Holiness unmakes before it heals, not because God enjoys the demolition but because you cannot pour a footing on top of a house.

Here is what I cannot stop thinking about, all these years after I first read Isaiah 6 as an unbeliever and felt it watching me. The seraphim have not stopped. The song was old when Isaiah heard it and it is running now, at this hour, while you hold this book. Holy, holy, holy is not a hymn about God. It is the weather around him. The only question is whether the rooms we worship in every Sunday are, in any sense their architecture or their liturgy or their preacher would admit, downwind of it. The doorposts still shake somewhere. It is our thresholds that have gone still.
reflect: Isaiah confessed unclean lips, the sin braided into his gift. If holiness went looking in your best thing rather than your worst, what would it find?
Only holiness is raised to the third power in Scripture, never love or mercy. What does that weighting suggest about how God describes himself?
Have you ever been genuinely undone, by God or by truth arriving from anywhere? What survived the unmaking, and what did not deserve to?
Bell says we send people who have never been undone and then study why leaders collapse. Where have you watched that sequence fail?

chapters.title: Who Then Is This
chapters.summary: The claim that Jesus corrected the fierce God of the Old Testament is an old heresy with a name, and Mark 4 dismantles it. The disciples feared the calm more than the storm. Bell holds the whip and the woes together with the bruised reed and the touched leper, and finds not niceness but precision, severity toward the proud and tenderness toward the crushed.
chapters.body:
There is a move everyone makes at this point in the argument, and I want to say it out loud so we can watch it fail. The move goes like this. Yes, the Old Testament God is fierce, the bush and the mountain and the smoke, all granted. But then Jesus came and showed us what God is really like, and Jesus is gentle, so the fierceness was the rough draft and the gentleness is the final edition. It sounds like reverence for Christ. It is actually a very old heresy with a very specific name. Around the year 144, a wealthy shipowner named Marcion stood before the church in Rome and argued exactly this, that the creator God of the Hebrew Scriptures, the God of law and judgment, was a lesser and darker being than the Father of Jesus Christ, and that a faithful church should cut the two apart, keep the kind God, and let the fierce one go. The church heard him out and excommunicated him, and returned his donation, and spent the next generation writing against him, because it understood that a Jesus severed from Sinai is not a purer Christianity. He is a different god altogether. Most of us have never heard Marcion's name. We have simply inherited his scissors, and much of the American church is functionally Marcionite without the courage of his paperwork, fierce God retired, nice Jesus installed.

The cure for this is not an argument. It is the text. So come stand in the boat.

Mark 4 ends a long day of teaching. Evening comes, and Jesus says, let us go across to the other side, and they take him with them in the boat, just as he was, which is Mark's way of saying exhausted. And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. The Sea of Galilee sits in a bowl of hills that funnels cold wind down onto warm water without warning, and at least four of the men in that boat were professional fishermen on their home lake. This detail matters. These are not tourists panicking at spray. When Peter and Andrew and James and John conclude that they are going to die, that is an expert assessment of the conditions. And Jesus, in the stern, is asleep on the cushion. The Lord of the storm, unbothered by the storm, with the specificity of an eyewitness memory, on the cushion.

They wake him, and their question is the question of every sufferer who has ever prayed into the wind. Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing. Note that they do not ask him to do anything. There is nothing, in their inventory of the possible, that a carpenter can do about weather. They wake him, I think, because dying alone is worse, and because the sleeping looked like not caring, and the accusation in their voice is the same one we make politely in church and honestly in the car. And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, peace, be still. Mark's Greek is blunter, muzzle yourself, the word you would use on an animal. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

Now comes the sentence this whole chapter exists for. He said to them, why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith? And they were filled with great fear. Read it again, slowly, because we have sanded this scene into a bedtime story and the text is not one. The storm is over. The danger is gone. The lake is glass. And now they are afraid, more afraid than the weather ever made them, and Mark writes it as literally as Greek allows, they feared a great fear. And they said to one another, who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

Here is what the boat teaches, and I have never found it taught better anywhere in Scripture. The storm could only kill them. The man in the stern was something worse than death and better than rescue, both at once. A storm threatens your life, and your life is a thing you always knew you would lose someday. The man who muzzles a storm with a sentence threatens your categories, your entire map of what can be in the world and what cannot, and a man will cling to his map long after he has given up on his life. That is why the great fear comes after the great calm. They had prayed to a teacher for sympathy, and the prayer was answered by the voice that said let there be, and the answer to who then is this had been given centuries earlier by a psalmist describing the LORD, who made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed. The disciples got exactly what the nice god promises, rescue, comfort, safety. And the delivery of it undid them, because the one delivering it was not nice. He was God in a boat, and there is no comfortable way to be in a boat with God.

Was Jesus gentle. Yes, with a gentleness that still has no rival in the literature of any civilization, and we will stand in that gentleness before this chapter ends. But first the other exhibits, because the church has been running a public relations campaign on his behalf that he never authorized. This is the man who made a whip of cords, John tells us, and drove the livestock dealers and the money-changers out of the temple courts, overturning their tables, scattering their coins, his disciples remembering the psalm, zeal for your house will consume me. Making a whip takes time. This was not a flash of temper. It was a considered act of prophetic violence against a religious economy, performed by the Prince of Peace. This is the man who called the most respected religious leaders of his nation whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of dead men's bones within, who called them serpents and a brood of vipers and asked them how they expected to escape being sentenced to hell. When his disciples came to him, worried, and said, do you know the Pharisees were offended by what you said, he answered that every plant his Father had not planted would be rooted up, and let them be, blind guides. He knew he had offended. He declined to fix it. This is the man who watched a crowd of thousands walk away in John 6 after a sermon he knew they could not stomach, and did not run after them with a clarification, but turned to the twelve and asked, do you want to go away as well? This is the man who said that anyone who does not take up his cross and follow him cannot be his disciple. Nobody nice has ever said that sentence. Nobody nice has ever meant it.

And this same man, the whip still in living memory, is the one of whom Matthew says, quoting Isaiah, a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench. This is the man who touched the leper before healing him, when a word would have done it from a safe distance, because a man untouched for years needed the hand as much as the cure. The man who felt power go out of him in a crush of bodies and stopped everything to find the one trembling woman who had touched his robe, and called her daughter, the only person in the Gospels he ever addressed by that name. The man who received children when the disciples were shooing them off, who forgave a woman the law was ready to stone and a thief the empire was in the act of executing, who wept at a tomb he was about to empty. The gentleness is real, as real as the whip, and here is the pattern that resolves them, because there is a pattern, and once you see it you can never unsee it. His severity runs toward the strong, the certain, the religiously armored, the self-sufficient. His tenderness runs toward the crushed, the failing, the exposed, the ones out of arguments. He is never once cruel to the broken and never once flattering to the proud, and he never confuses the two, not one time in four Gospels. Niceness cannot do this. Niceness is indiscriminate, it smiles at everyone equally because its real job is the comfort of the one smiling. Jesus is not indiscriminate. Jesus is precise, the way a surgeon is precise, and the blade and the suture are the same hand.

Both of our tribes take their scissors to this pattern, and both should be named. The therapeutic church keeps the bruised reed and files the whip under cultural context, producing a Christ of infinite affirmation who would never root up anything, a Mister Rogers of Nazareth who could not conceivably have been crucified, because no empire executes a man for niceness. The fighting church keeps the whip and loses the reed, producing a culture-war Christ, all temple tables and no touched lepers, a mascot for hardness that the actual Jesus would have called a whitewashed tomb, since hardness toward the broken was the one thing that reliably drew his anger. Same scissors, opposite halves, and the two counterfeit Christs sell out their respective rooms every Sunday while the whole one stands outside, harder than the one and gentler than the other, knocking.

C.S. Lewis put the whole matter into the mouth of a talking beaver in 1950, and it remains the best single sentence about God written in the last century. In The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, the children, hearing that Aslan is a lion, ask nervously whether he is safe, and Mr. Beaver answers that of course he is not safe. But he is good. Safe is a question about what a thing can do to you. Good is a question about what a thing is. The disciples in the boat learned the difference in one evening, on glass-calm water, with their hearts hammering. They were never safe with him again in any sense their old maps could recognize, and they followed him out of that boat to eleven martyrdoms and one exile, which is not the biography of men who had found a nice teacher. It is the biography of men who had met the question, who then is this, and spent the rest of their lives inside the answer. That question is now yours, and the storm-calmed sea will not answer it for you, and neither will I. He is not safe. He is not nice. He is good, and the difference between those words is the difference between the religion we manufactured and the man who is actually there.
reflect: The disciples were more afraid after the rescue than during the danger. What does their fear of the calm reveal that our picture of Jesus usually omits?
Bell claims Jesus is never cruel to the broken and never flattering to the proud. Test that pattern against the Gospel scenes you know best. Does it hold?
Which half of Jesus does your tribe keep, the whip or the reed, and what does the discarded half say about what your tribe is protecting?
Mr. Beaver said Aslan is not safe, but he is good. Why do we keep trying to collapse those two words into one?

chapters.title: What the Small God Costs
chapters.summary: The audit of the trade. The nice god empties the cross, shrinks worship to appreciation and prayer to self-talk, deflates sin until forgiveness has nothing to forgive, evaporates at the graveside, bores the honest skeptic, and hands the next generation a religion they complete by leaving. The small god was never a gain. He was a receipt.
chapters.body:
We talk about the nice god as though he were a gain. That is the language of the trade, the story we tell about ourselves, that we matured past the frightening God of our grandparents into a warmer and truer faith, the way a family outgrows a superstition. Nobody audits a gain. So this chapter is the audit, the honest accounting of what the small god actually costs, line by line, because I have come to believe he is not a gain at all. He is an amputation that we have learned to call a graduation, and the bill for him arrives in the mail of every life eventually, and it is enormous.

Start at the center, with the cross, because that is the first thing the nice god bankrupts. Run the logic without flinching. If God was never truly holy, if his standard was never actually lethal, if his justice was never really going to fall on anyone, then what, precisely, happened at Golgotha. What was forgiven, and at what cost, and why the blood. Why the agony in the garden, the sweat falling like drops of blood, the prayer that the cup might pass. Why the cry of dereliction, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. If the Father was always basically agreeable, always going to wave it through, then the crucifixion is not a rescue. It is theater, and grotesque theater, God torturing himself to solve a problem that did not exist. The nice god empties the cross of its meaning and leaves the church holding the most violent symbol in human history with nothing to say about it except that it shows how much God cares. Which is true. And infinitely thin. And not remotely enough to build a life on, let alone to explain why the event sits at the hinge of history with a torn curtain behind it. Grace is only amazing if there was wrath to be carried. Forgiveness is only costly if there was a debt. A church that has quietly retired the holiness of God will find, sooner or later, that it has also retired the gospel, and is left performing the memory of a rescue from nothing.

The second line on the bill is worship. Worship is the response of a small thing to a vast one, the creature's answer to weight, and you cannot worship what you can manage. You can only appreciate it. And appreciation is what we have, sanctuaries full of people who appreciate God, who are grateful in his general direction, who find the music moving and the message helpful. I do not sneer at any of that, but I have stood on the platform and I know the difference between a room that is moved and a room that is undone, and I know which one the seraphim are in. When the object shrinks, the response shrinks with it, mathematically, and no production value on earth can put the weight back. We keep trying to engineer transcendence with lights and reverb, and the trying is itself the confession. You do not need a fog machine at Sinai. Weight is a lost experience among us not because God got smaller but because the god we actually hold in our minds while we sing got smaller, and the body always knows.

Third, prayer. Under the nice god, prayer degrades into self-talk with a devotional accent, the buffered self addressing its own kindest voice and calling the echo God. Real petition is an act of daring. It assumes a God who is actually there, actually free, actually able, a God who might say no, which is the possibility that makes yes mean something. The nice god cannot refuse you anything because he was built to have no will that crosses yours, and a god who cannot refuse cannot really give. He can only reflect. That is why prayer to him so quickly becomes exhausting or empty, a wellness practice we defend with studies about its benefits, and why the praying of the saints was so different, Moses arguing on the mountain, Hannah pouring herself out at Shiloh, Jesus sweating in the garden until an angel came. Those people were contending with someone. We are journaling at someone, and somewhere inside we know it.

Fourth, sin, and with it the entire machinery of moral seriousness. The nice god cannot afford the word, so under his administration sin softens into mistakes, brokenness, struggles, language that happens to a person rather than language a person is responsible for. And this feels like kindness, and it is actually a theft, because you cannot be forgiven more deeply than you are guilty. Shallow guilt, shallow grace, that is the exchange rate, fixed, non-negotiable. When we lowered the diagnosis to spare people's feelings, we lowered the cure to match, and then we wondered why absolution stopped landing, why people sat through a thousand assurances of pardon and still carried their shame home in the same bag, and the answer is that you cannot pardon what you refused to name. The old liturgies made people say the terrible words out loud, we have sinned against you in thought, word, and deed, and then, and only then, spoke Christ's forgiveness over them, and people walked out light. We deleted the first half as bad for morale and have spent decades wondering where the lightness went.

Fifth, and this is the line item that empties families out of churches, suffering. A faith that has never been asked to carry anything cannot suddenly carry everything, and every life eventually asks its faith to carry everything. I told you in the first chapter about a man in my congregation, and I will keep the details behind the veil where they belong, but the shape of it belongs to this argument. He was a good man with a warm faith composed almost entirely of the nice god, God loved him, God was beside him, God wanted good things for him, all of it true and none of it weight-bearing. Then his daughter died, young and wrong, and I sat with him through the worst of it, and I watched his faith come apart, and I need you to see what I saw. It did not come apart because his god was too harsh. It came apart because his god was too small. The nice god had nothing to say at that graveside. The nice god could only stand there and feel sad, and a god who can only feel sad is no better than the rest of us feeling sad, and slightly worse, because we had advertised him as more. Drowning men do not rescue each other. What that man needed was the God of terrible sovereignty and terrible mercy, the God who is Lord even of the grave, whose refusal to explain himself in the whirlwind is somehow more comforting than every explanation, the God who does not stand beside death wringing his hands but holds its keys. He had traded that God away years before, an ounce at a time, in a thousand comfortable Sundays, some of them in my church, under my preaching. When the cold came, the warm god evaporated. That is what he does. He is a fair-weather deity, built in the surplus of a comfortable society, and he has no equipment for catastrophe, and the day you finally need a god is the day you find out which one you have.

Sixth, the skeptic, and here I speak from the years when I was one. The nice god costs the church its credibility with every serious unbeliever, because serious unbelievers can smell a manufactured deity at a hundred yards. A god who agrees with his owners about everything, who evolves on schedule with their politics, who demands nothing they were not already inclined to do, is so obviously a product of his market that no argument for him is required, and none was ever offered to me that did not embarrass us both. I did not disbelieve in the God of the Bible because he was too strange to credit. Strangeness, I could have respected. The god I disbelieved in was too convenient to credit. If Christians had shown me their actual God, the one in the whirlwind, the one on the cross, the one who unmade Isaiah, I would still have had my arguments, but I would have been facing something with edges I could not have invented, and edges, to an honest atheist, are evidence. Not proof. Evidence of otherness, of something that is not simply us talking to ourselves. The church that sanded off every edge to make God easier to accept made him, for people like me, impossible to take seriously. You cannot offend a skeptic into the kingdom, but you cannot bore him into it either, and niceness is boring, and we have been boring for fifty years.

Seventh, the children, which is where the whole audit lands with a thud. The generation raised on Moralistic Therapeutic Deism did not rebel against it. That is the detail everyone misses when they wring their hands about the young leaving church. They did not reject what we taught them. They completed it. If God's role is to underwrite my happiness and require my niceness, then once the culture supplies both without the early alarm and the offering envelope, church attendance becomes what it now statistically is, optional equipment on a life already headed where it was going. The nice god was supposed to be the low, welcoming doorway into the deeper faith. He turned out to be the exit, marked and lit, and our children walked through it in the largest numbers of any generation in American history, politely, without anger, the way you leave a store where nothing was worth the price. They were promised the god of their own flourishing, and they kept the flourishing and dropped the god, and the terrible thing is that this was the rational response to what we actually taught.

Add up the lines. A cross with no meaning, worship with no weight, prayer with no listener, guilt with no absolution, suffering with no floor beneath it, skeptics with nothing to respect, children with nothing to keep. That is the price of the small god, and we paid it in installments, which is why it never felt like a purchase. No one would have traded the Lord of hosts for this in a single transaction. We traded him a Sunday at a time, a softened sermon at a time, an ounce of weight at a time, each ounce reasonable, each ounce pastoral, until the scale read zero and we stood in a room we had built ourselves, warm, well-lit, and empty of everything that could hold us. The nice god was never a gain. He was never even a god. He was a receipt, and this chapter is just the sum at the bottom, and the sum is everything.
chapters.verdict: A god you can manage cannot hold you.
reflect: If God was never truly holy, what exactly happened at the cross? Try to answer without borrowing anything from the God this book says we traded away.
You cannot be forgiven more deeply than you were guilty. Where have you experienced the exchange rate between shallow diagnosis and shallow grace?
Bell says the young did not reject Moralistic Therapeutic Deism, they completed it. Does that account fit the people you know who left the church?
What is your faith currently being asked to carry, and what is the heaviest thing it has ever actually held?

chapters.title: Cheap Grace
chapters.summary: Bonhoeffer at depth. Writing in 1937 out of an outlawed seminary in a church that had saluted Hitler, he named the disease that made the surrender possible, grace we bestow on ourselves, the justification of sin without the justification of the sinner. Cheap grace and the nice god are the same object seen from two angles, and the disease wears a flag as easily as a smile.
chapters.body:
In the summer of 1937, in Nazi Germany, the Gestapo closed a small illegal seminary in Pomerania at Finkenwalde, where a thirty-one-year-old theologian named Dietrich Bonhoeffer had spent two years training pastors for a church in resistance. That November, Bonhoeffer published the book he had been writing out of that community, Nachfolge, known to English readers as The Cost of Discipleship. To understand why that book still burns, you have to understand what it was written against. Four years earlier, in 1933, the movement calling itself the German Christians had swept the church elections and set about fusing the cross with the swastika, a church of the nation, purged and coordinated and useful. A minority resisted. At Barmen in May 1934 the Confessing Church declared that Jesus Christ, and no earthly leader and no national destiny, is the one Word of God the church must hear and obey. Bonhoeffer belonged to that resistance, and Finkenwalde was its seminary, and the question underneath his book was the question underneath the ruins of his church. How does a nation of baptized people, catechized people, churchgoing Lutheran people, hand itself to a devil by acclamation. His answer was not political. It was theological, and it is aimed at us. The disaster was possible, he argued, because the church had spent generations dispensing something he called cheap grace.

Cheap grace, he wrote in 1937, is grace we bestow on ourselves. It is the preaching of forgiveness without repentance, communion without confession, grace without the cross. Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of the church, he said, and we are fighting today for costly grace. Read that first sentence again, because everything is in it. Grace we bestow on ourselves. Not grace God gives, grace we administer, self-service pardon, the doctrine of forgiveness converted into a standing account from which the sinner makes his own withdrawals. Under cheap grace, Bonhoeffer argued, grace is no longer the living voice of God addressing a particular man and calling him out of his life. It is a principle, a general truth, a system. The world discovers in it a cheap covering for its sins, no contrition required, no real desire to be freed from them, and the church becomes the dispensary. And he pressed the diagnosis to its sharpest possible point in a distinction I have never escaped since the first time I read it. Cheap grace is the justification of the sin without the justification of the sinner. Sit with that sentence, because it divides the world. Real grace justifies the sinner, kills him and makes him alive, takes a man and remakes him. Cheap grace justifies the sin, blesses the man exactly as he is, requires nothing to die, and leaves as its product a forgiven life in which nothing whatever has changed, a Christian indistinguishable from his neighbor except for the hour he keeps on Sunday.
