Germany, Bonhoeffer said, had been covered with such Christians like a field with stubble, and when the fire came through, they burned.

Against this he set what he called costly grace. Costly grace is the treasure hidden in the field, for the sake of which a man goes and sells all that he has. It is the pearl of great price, the call of Jesus Christ at which the disciple leaves his nets and follows. It is costly, he wrote, because it costs a man his life, and it is grace because it gives him the only true life. It is costly because it condemns sin, and grace because it justifies the sinner. And above everything, it is costly because it cost God the life of his Son, and what has cost God so dearly cannot be cheap for us. There is the whole book, and there is the whole argument of the book you are holding, met from the other direction. When Bonhoeffer summarized the call of Christ, he did it in a sentence that has become famous enough to be numb, and I want you to hear it as the sober piece of theology it is and not as a poster. The call of Jesus, he said, is a call to come and die. He meant that grace, real grace, is not the exemption from discipleship. It is the enlistment. The forgiveness and the following are one event, and a church that separates them, offering the pardon while waiving the call, is not offering a gentler Christianity. It is offering a different substance entirely, wearing the sacraments of the true one.

Now bring the two halves of this book together, because this is the hinge, and I said in the first chapter that I would press on it. Cheap grace and the nice god are the same object seen from two angles. Run it both directions and watch it hold. A cheap grace requires a nice god to dispense it, a god with no holiness that had to be satisfied, no wrath that had to be borne, no cost sunk into the pardon, because if the holiness were real the grace could not be self-administered, you would need the coal and the altar and the cross. And a nice god can only ever offer cheap grace, because he has nothing costlier in stock, no fire out of which a costly mercy could come, nothing behind the smile. They stand together and they fall together. Smith and Denton found the god. Bonhoeffer, seventy years earlier, had already described the grace such a god would sell, and the kind of church it would produce, and what would become of that church when history finally asked it a hard question.

And here is where Bonhoeffer breaks the frame of every tribe that tries to quote him, and why he sits at the center of this book. We have been examining the therapeutic church, the church that went soft, and it would be easy to hear cheap grace as a diagnosis of softness. But look at the patient Bonhoeffer was actually treating. The German church of 1933 was not therapeutic. It was nationalist, muscular, flag-draped, full of talk about strength and destiny and the soul of the Volk. And Bonhoeffer's verdict was that this church had fallen to the strongman precisely because its grace was cheap, because two centuries of forgiveness without repentance had produced Christians with no spine that costs anything, a church that had never asked its people to die to anything and therefore could not ask them to stand against anything. Cheap grace is not a disease of soft churches. It is a disease of churches, and it wears whatever the culture is wearing. In Weimar it wore a uniform. In America it wears a smile, and in some of our sanctuaries it wears the flag exactly as it did in 1933, and the two congregations that despise each other across our political divide are often running the identical transaction at the identical altar, pardon without repentance, comfort without cost, a god who asks nothing of me and everything of my enemies. The therapeutic church bestows cheap grace on the self, no repentance required of my choices. The nationalist church bestows cheap grace on the tribe, no repentance required of my side, my history, my rage. Same product. Same price. Same ending, eventually, when the fire comes through.

I have to be fair to the doctrine that cheap grace corrupts, because the counterfeit works only because the original is real, and there are readers of this chapter who grew up under preaching that made them earn what Christ had already bought, and they need to hear this part. Grace alone is not the error. Grace alone is the gospel. When Luther nailed his theses to the door at Wittenberg in 1517, the recovery of free grace was the recovery of Christianity itself, and Bonhoeffer, a Lutheran to his bones, said so plainly. His argument was historical and it was devastating. Luther's grace was costly because it came at the end of the monastery, the anguish, the whole failed project of self-justification collapsing before it was surrendered. Luther knew, in his body, what the pardon had rescued him from. But his heirs, Bonhoeffer said, inherited the conclusion without the struggle, the verdict without the trial. What Luther had learned on his knees was repeated from lecterns as a premise, and within generations the costliest sentence in the world, the sinner is justified by grace alone, had been ground down into its own opposite, a reason nothing needs to change. That is how the best doctrines die, not by refutation but by inheritance, passed to people who paid nothing for them. And it is the precise biography of the American evangelical gospel I was handed to preach, born in revival fire, worn smooth by transmission, arriving in my generation as a technique for closing a decision, pray this prayer, mean it sincerely, your eternity is settled and your Tuesday is your own. Grace as transaction. Grace as exemption. Grace we bestow on ourselves, at the front of the room, in the last five minutes, to music.

I have dispensed it. Let me say it without softening, since the whole argument of this chapter is that softening is the disease. I have preached forgiveness without repentance because repentance slows the service down. I have served communion without confession to people I knew, pastorally, personally, were living in open war with each other, because the alternative was a scene. I have preached funerals where I settled a man's eternal account from the pulpit on no evidence the man ever presented, because his family was in the second row and grace was the kind thing to say. Every one of those moments felt like mercy. Every one was theft, because what I handed out in those moments cost me nothing and cost them nothing, and we all walked out with the receipt for a treasure no one had bought. What has cost God so dearly cannot be cheap for us. I believed that sentence the whole time. I just did not preach like it, because costly grace empties rooms, and cheap grace fills them, and I liked full rooms. We will stand in that confession properly two chapters from now.

Bonhoeffer was hanged at Flossenburg concentration camp on April 9, 1945, weeks before the end of the war in Europe, for his part in the resistance against Hitler. He was thirty-nine. The camp doctor who watched him die recorded that he had never seen a man go to death so composed, so entirely at peace. I do not bring his death in to decorate the chapter. I bring it in because it is the proof of the argument. Cheap grace produces Christians who cannot stand against anything, and costly grace produced a man who could kneel in prayer and then climb the scaffold, because the call to come and die had never been news to him. He had answered it years before, in a lecture hall, in a seminary the state had outlawed, in ten thousand small deaths of preference and safety and career, so that the last one, when it came, was only the old obedience one more time. His church, the respectable one, the one with the full sanctuaries and the reasonable sermons and the grace that asked for nothing, made its peace with the regime that killed him. We quote him now, warmly, in churches on both sides of every American divide, churches he would have looked at long and hard. The quoting is easy. It is grace we bestow on ourselves.
chapters.verdict: Grace that costs nothing buys nothing.
reflect: Bonhoeffer distinguished the justification of the sinner from the justification of the sin. In your own life, which one have you more often received, and which have you more often wanted?
The German church that fell to Hitler was not soft. It was strong and flag-draped. What does it mean that cheap grace produced that church rather than a timid one?
Where does your tribe, political or theological, receive pardon without repentance? Where do you?
What has your faith actually cost you? If the honest answer is nothing, what would Bonhoeffer say you are holding?

chapters.title: The Severe Mercy
chapters.summary: Hebrews 12 unfolded by a man who was raised without a father and is raising five sons. The mark of abandonment is not hardship but the absence of correction, and the discipline of God is a surgeon's knife, not a mugger's, aimed at a wholeness we have not seen. The severe mercy is a testimony you may give about your own wound and never about anyone else's.
chapters.body:
Two men come toward you holding knives. One is a mugger and one is a surgeon, and everything, absolutely everything, depends on which is which, and yet notice what the difference is not. The difference is not the knife. It is not the cutting, and it is not even the pain, because the surgeon may hurt you far more than the mugger and for longer. The difference is intent, and skill, and what you are worth to the man holding the blade. We know this in medicine so deeply that no one calls a surgeon violent. And then we come to the discipline of God, and the whole culture, including most of the church, loses the distinction completely, and decides that a God who cuts must be a God who mugs, and flees to a god who would never cut, and calls him kind. But a god who never cuts is not kinder. He has simply stopped operating. The question this chapter asks is the one we have been circling since the boat, and it is time to ask it directly. When God hurts you, what is he doing.

The New Testament answers that question most fully in the twelfth chapter of Hebrews, in a letter written to believers who were suffering and thinking about quitting. These were people who had endured public shaming and the plundering of their property for the name of Christ, and the temptation eating at them was not atheism. It was drift, the quiet slide back toward an easier religion. And the author, having spent eleven chapters building the case that Christ is greater than everything they would trade him for, turns in chapter twelve to their pain, and says the thing no therapeutic culture can hear without flinching. He quotes Proverbs 3, the old wisdom of the covenant. My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.

The argument that follows runs entirely through fatherhood, and it runs uphill against everything our reflexes tell us. It is for discipline that you have to endure, the author writes. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? And then the inversion that turns the whole passage over. If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons. Do not read past that. The writer of Hebrews says that the mark of abandonment is not the presence of hardship in your life. It is the absence of correction. The father who never disciplines is not the kind one. He is the one who has quietly disowned you without filing the paperwork, the one whose indulgence is indifference wearing indulgence's clothes. Every parent knows a version of this at street level. The child nobody ever corrects is not the loved child. He is the child nobody is willing to pay the cost of loving, because correction is expensive, it costs conflict and consistency and the risk of being hated by someone whose love you want, and only a parent who intends to keep the child pays it.

I have to walk carefully here, and personally, because I came to this passage with a wound where the analogy should be. I was raised without a father. What I knew of fathers, for the whole first stretch of my life, was absence, and the reader who shares that history knows what it does to every scripture that begins, my son. For years, even after my conversion, the discipline passages read to me as menace, because I had no memory of correction that came from a man who stayed. Correction, in my experience, was what the leaving kind of man did on his way out the door. A man with no father reads Hebrews 12 the way a man with no country reads an anthem, moved and locked out at once. So I understand, from inside, why a generation of the fatherless and the badly fathered built a god who would never discipline anyone. They were not being shallow. They were guarding a wound. If the only knives you have ever seen were muggers' knives, a surgeon is just a mugger with better lighting, and you will run from him too, and you will be wise to, by every light you have.

Then God gave me five sons, and I learned the passage from the other side of it, which is the only place I could have learned it. I discipline my sons. I do it badly some days, in impatience, and I have had to apologize on my knees to a boy more than once, so this is not a chapter written by the father who got it right. But I know now, in my body, what I could never have learned as an argument, that correction is a function of intention. I correct my sons because I intend to keep them. Because I am planning on their fortieth birthdays. Because I can see down the road of a particular habit to the man it builds, and I love the man too much to let the habit go unchallenged. The father who shrugs is not the gentle one. Shrugging is the cheapest thing a father can do, and my own absence-shaped childhood taught me its exact price. When Hebrews says the Lord disciplines the one he loves, it is not describing a divine temper. It is describing a Father with plans, a Father who has seen your fortieth birthday and your ten-thousandth, and who is building, in you, now, at cost, the person who can live there.

Because look at what the passage says the discipline is for. He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. There is the destination, stated flatly, and it is not our comfort and it is not even our morality. It is his holiness, shared, the fire of the bush somehow made native to the creature, the thing Isaiah was undone by somehow made the air we can finally breathe. God is not raising nice children. He is raising children who can bear his presence and be glad in it, and between what I am on any given Tuesday and that creature stands a distance that only surgery crosses. And then the writer says the truest sentence about pain in all of Scripture, the one that separates the biblical faith from every religion of immediate consolation. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. For the moment, painful. Later, peaceful fruit. The entire logic of the passage hangs on that word later, and later is precisely the word the therapeutic age has lost the ability to hear. A culture organized around present well-being has no category for a good that arrives on the far side of a pain that will not be shortened. The surgeon lives in later. The therapist, by the nature of the office, mostly works in now. And God, Hebrews insists, is doing the surgeon's work, cutting with reference to a wholeness we have not seen yet, and the peaceful fruit is real, and it is fruit, which means it grows at the speed of orchards and not at the speed of relief.

In 1977 a man named Sheldon Vanauken published a memoir called A Severe Mercy, about the death of his young wife Davy and the correspondence he carried on with his friend C.S. Lewis through the grief. It was Lewis who gave him the phrase. Lewis wrote to Vanauken that the death he was living through was a severe mercy, and Vanauken spent the rest of the book, and in some ways the rest of his life, weighing those two words that have no business standing together. He came to believe that what he lost had done for him what no gentleness ever could, that he and Davy had built a love so complete it had quietly closed itself against God, and that the breaking of it was the breaking open of him. I hand you that phrase with both hands and a warning, because it is holy ground and people get hurt here. The severe mercy is a testimony, not an explanation. It is a sentence you are permitted to say, slowly, after years, about your own wound. It is never, ever a sentence you are permitted to say about someone else's. The friends of Job tried to run this arithmetic on another man's catastrophe, confidently, theologically, and at the end of that book God says his wrath burns against them, for they have not spoken of him what is right. Scripture itself forbids the move. Not every suffering is a lesson. Not every loss is a scalpel. Some things are just the ruin of a broken world, and the same Bible that gives us Hebrews 12 gives us a Christ who stood at a tomb and wept, and did not explain.

So how do you tell them apart, the mugger's knife and the surgeon's. Mostly, from inside the moment, you cannot, and I will not insult you by pretending otherwise. But the gospel changes the one thing that can be changed, which is what you know about the one holding the blade. Here is the fixed point, and everything in this chapter hangs from it. For those who are in Christ, punishment is off the table. Not softened. Off the table, finished, spent at the cross, because there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Whatever the pain in your life is doing, it is not the settling of accounts, because the account was settled outside the city wall two thousand years ago. What remains is not tribunal but training, and I do not pretend the difference makes the cutting hurt less. It does not. It makes the cutting mean differently, and meaning is what human beings actually run on. The same pain that is unbearable as a sentence becomes bearable, barely, as surgery, and the whole difference is the face above the knife.

I told you my conversion was not gentle, and I can say now what I could not say then. Losing my unbelief was the first surgery. It cost me the self I had built, the clear-eyed man who had life figured out, a decade of certainty, some friendships that never recovered, my whole standing in my own eyes. For the moment, and the moment lasted months, it seemed only painful. I could not have written the word mercy anywhere near it. Later, and only later, it yielded. Everything I now am that is worth anything, the faith, the marriage, the five sons raised by a man determined to break the inheritance of absence, the church I serve, grew in the field that pain cleared. I say that about my own wound, as testimony, the only way it is allowed to be said. The severe mercy is real. The surgeon is real, and he is your Father, and he is not punishing you, and he does not waste pain, and later is coming. That is everything I know about suffering after fifteen years of pastoring through other people's worst days, and I have watched it hold men who had nothing else left to stand on, and it held.
reflect: Hebrews says the child left without discipline is the unloved one. How does that inversion sit against your own experience of fathers, good or absent?
The passage hangs on the word later. What in your life is currently painful rather than pleasant, and what would it mean to trust the orchard speed of its fruit?
Bell insists the severe mercy may never be spoken over someone else's grave. Why does the same sentence heal in the first person and wound in the second?
If punishment is truly off the table for those in Christ, how does that change the meaning of the hardest thing you are carrying right now?

chapters.title: The Fear of the LORD
chapters.summary: Scripture commands fear not and calls fear the beginning of wisdom, and Moses says both in one sentence. Bell takes the strongest objection, fear as clerical control with 1 John 4:18 in its hand, then recovers the old distinction between the slave's fear and the son's, and Psalm 130's strange claim that forgiveness itself produces the trembling. Rightly feared, every lesser fear loses its throne.
chapters.body:
The Bible's most repeated command is some form of fear not. The Bible's most repeated definition of wisdom is that it begins with fear. Both of those statements are true, both are easy to verify, and the whole spiritual condition of the modern church can be diagnosed by which of the two it can still hear. We have built entire theologies out of fear not. We have hung it in nurseries and printed it on mugs, and it belongs there, it is the tender word of God to the terrified, spoken by angels and by Christ himself more often than almost anything else. But Scripture will not let the comfort stand alone, and neither will Moses, who fused the two commands into a single sentence at the foot of Sinai and left it there for us like a knot we are required to untie. The people have just heard the voice of God and begged for it to stop, and Moses says to them, do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin. Do not fear, so that you may fear. One breath, both commands, from the man who spoke with God face to face. Any account of the fear of the LORD that cannot hold that sentence intact is not an account of it at all, and the nice god was invented, in large part, by people who could not hold it, and I do not blame them, and I am going to try to hold it now.

First, the objection, and I want it at full strength, because it is the best objection in this book and it comes armed with a verse. Fear, says the skeptic, is the oldest tool of religious control ever forged. Frighten a child about hell early enough and you own his conscience for life, and priesthoods of every faith have known this and used it, and the wreckage is real, and some of it sits in the pews of my own church, adults still flinching from a childhood deity who watched them the way a cat watches a hole. And the wounded believer joins the skeptic here, holding 1 John 4:18, and it says what it says. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love. There it is, canonical, apostolic. If the fear of God means trembling before a punisher, then John declares that love's whole business is to abolish it. Whatever the fear of the LORD is, it cannot be that, or the Bible is at war with itself.

The old theologians untied this knot centuries ago, and their distinction, worked out from Augustine onward, remains the sharpest tool anyone has offered. They distinguished servile fear from filial fear, the fear of the slave from the fear of the son. Servile fear is the slave's calculation before the lash, dread of punishment from a power that does not love you, and its object is the pain, and its fruit is hiding, and its logic is escape. That is the fear John says perfect love casts out, because it has to do with punishment, and punishment, we saw in the last chapter, is precisely what the cross has taken off the table. But filial fear is a different creature with the same name. It is the fear of the son who is loved and knows it, the dread not of what the father will do to you but of what you might do to him, the trembling care of someone holding a relationship whose worth he finally sees. Its object is not the pain. Its object is the grief of the beloved, and its fruit is not hiding but carefulness, and its logic is not escape but honor. The slave fears the father's hand. The son fears the father's sorrow. Same word, opposite directions, and the whole biblical doctrine lives in the second one.

If you doubt that Scripture itself makes this distinction, the Psalter closes the case with the strangest verse in it. Psalm 130, out of the depths, builds to this. But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared. Read it twice, because it runs exactly backward to every instinct we have. Not, with you there is forgiveness, that you may be loved, or approached, or relaxed around. Feared. The psalmist says that forgiveness produces fear, that mercy is the very thing that teaches trembling. How. Stand inside the experience and it opens. As long as God is only a punisher, you fear him the servile way, and the fear caps out at the size of your self-interest. But the day you are actually forgiven, really forgiven, the debt you know was real simply carried away, two things are revealed at once, the holiness that made the debt matter and the love that paid it, and the creature who sees both at the same time does not relax. He trembles, worse than before and completely differently, the way a man pardoned from the gallows trembles at his pardoner, not because he might still hang but because he has just seen what he was worth to someone. Cheap grace produces relief, which fades. Costly grace produces filial fear, which lasts, because it is not a mood. It is an accurate perception of what just happened.

And accuracy, I have come to believe, is the deepest thing the fear of the LORD is. We treat fear as a feeling that distorts, and usually it is. But stand a man at the rim of the Grand Canyon at dusk and the catch in his chest is not a distortion. It is the correct registration of scale, the creature's instrument reading the size of what it faces, and we do not medicate it, we drive four hours for it. The fear of the LORD is that, aimed at last at the only object vast enough to deserve it. It is not an emotion added to reality. It is the sane reading of reality, the felt mathematics of being a creature of dust addressed by the One who spoke galaxies, and to lack it is not maturity. To lack it is to be wrong about the scale of things, the way a man strolling on a runway is wrong, however calm he feels. That is why Proverbs 9:10 says what it says. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight. Not the ceiling of wisdom, the beginning, the entry fee, the first accurate measurement from which every other measurement follows. A man who has God's size wrong has everything's size wrong, his money, his enemies, his death, his diagnosis, all of it misfiled, because the unit of measure at the bottom of his mind is off. Wisdom cannot begin until the scale is fixed, and the fixing of the scale, felt in the body, has a name, and the name is the fear of the LORD.

Which explains the strangest thing about the people who have it, a thing I have now watched for fifteen years of ministry. The fear of the LORD displaces every other fear. It does not add a terror to life. It evicts the tenants. Scripture says the fear of man lays a snare, and I have watched that snare hold men my whole life, good men, brave in every visible way, owned by the opinions of people who will not attend their funerals. Every human being fears something supremely, and the thing you fear supremely is your functional god, the throne does not sit empty. The man who fears the LORD is not fearless. He is rightly feared, feared-in-the-right-direction, and therefore he is the freest creature in any room, because the only opinion that can finally frighten him belongs to Someone who has already pardoned him. This is why the martyrs confound their executioners. This is why Bonhoeffer could climb the scaffold composed. Fear the LORD and you fear nothing else the same way again. Refuse to fear him, and it is not that you will fear nothing. You will fear everything, in rotation, forever, and I can verify that claim from the inside, because I know exactly what I fear in the weeks when my fear of God goes quiet. I fear the email. I fear the giving report. I fear the opinion of a man I do not even respect. The nice god cannot free you from any of that. He was built to lower the stakes, and he lowers them, and the vacated throne of fear does not stay vacant, it just gets occupied by whatever shouts loudest that week. A god you cannot tremble before leaves you trembling before everything else. That is the actual trade, and no one shows it to you at the counter.

And notice, finally, what the fear of the LORD does to the people in the text who have it, because it is the opposite of what we would predict. It does not drive them away from God. It drives them toward him. The same Israel that begged the voice to stop stood at the base of the mountain, but Moses, who feared God more than any man alive, drew near to the thick darkness where God was. The disciples in the boat, filled with great fear, did not swim for shore. They followed him to eleven executions. Isaiah, undone, volunteered. This is Otto's fascinans again, the magnetism inside the terror, and it is the final proof that filial fear and servile fear are different species. Servile fear runs. Filial fear kneels closer, trembling as it comes, because it has correctly perceived not only the size of God but the direction of his face, and the face is turned toward us, and the hand is open. The fear of the LORD is clean, says Psalm 19, enduring forever. Clean is the word I leave you with. There is a fear that dirties everything it touches, and I hope this chapter has helped you leave it behind for good. And there is a fear that washes, that clarifies, that sets every lesser thing back to its actual size and every trembling in the right direction, and the man who has never felt it has not yet met the God who is, only the god we made, who frightens no one, and holds no one, and was designed to do neither.
chapters.verdict: Rightly feared, the fear comes clean.
reflect: What do you actually fear supremely, measured by your sleepless nights rather than your theology? What does that fear currently govern in your life?
Psalm 130 says there is forgiveness with God, that he may be feared. Trace the logic in your own experience. Has mercy ever made you tremble?
How would you explain the difference between the fear that perfect love casts out and the fear that is the beginning of wisdom, to a teenager, in two sentences?
The people who feared God rightly in Scripture drew nearer, not further away. What would fearing in that direction look like for you this week?

chapters.title: The Pastor Who Preached Him
chapters.summary: The confession chapter. Bell names how the nice god came to be preached from his own pulpit in Fenton, not by decision but by feedback, sermon by softened sermon, sin rewritten as brokenness, judgment aimed only at people who were not in the room. The system that measures shepherds by attendance disciplines them toward the god who draws crowds, and the rooms were full.
chapters.body:
Every chapter so far has said we, and we was true, but we is also a place to hide. A man can confess the sins of American Christianity all day and sleep fine, because American Christianity is nobody's name. So this chapter retires the pronoun. I have been the pastor of First Baptist Church of Fenton, Michigan for the better part of fifteen years, and for a number of those years, more than I will get credit for admitting and fewer than my worst critic would guess, the god preached from my pulpit was the nice one, and I knew better, and I preached him anyway. This is the chapter about how that happens to a man who believes the Bible. I am writing it because I have never once heard it explained from inside, and because the explanation implicates a whole system, and because the system is still running, this Sunday, in tens of thousands of rooms.

Here is the first thing to understand. No pastor decides to preach the nice god. There is no morning a man stands at his desk and chooses the small deity over the Lord of hosts. What there is instead is feedback, and feedback is patient. Preach comfort, and the room warms. People linger at the door, the emails are kind, a family tells you they have finally found a church home. Preach holiness, wrath, repentance, judgment, and the room cools by two degrees, someone stiff shakes your hand without a word, and on Monday the email arrives, concerned, prayerful, cc'd to an elder. Nothing about any single week matters. But a preacher is trained by his congregation as surely as he trains them, one small reinforcement at a time, and the man does not feel himself moving because on any given week he has not moved, any more than a shoreline moves in an afternoon. I look back now at fifteen years of manuscripts, and I can read the erosion in them like rings in a tree. And I want to be precise about the mechanism, because it was not cowardice, or not mostly. It was something that wore the face of every pastoral virtue. It felt like love, not wanting to wound the fragile people in the third row. It felt like wisdom, not throwing red meat to controversy. It felt like strategy, keep them coming so they can hear the gospel eventually. Eventually has a way of not arriving. There is always a fragile person in the third row. There is always a reason this week is the wrong week for Isaiah 6, and after enough right reasons a man wakes up as the chaplain of people's self-regard and cannot name the Sunday it happened.

The second thing to understand is what gets measured, because what gets measured is what gets worshiped, in churches as surely as in corporations. In all my years of ministry, the wider church world has asked me one question about my congregation so many times that I could not begin to count it. How many are you running. Attendance. That is the metric, the sacrament of success, the number that gets a man invited to speak at the conference or quietly seated at the back of it. Nobody has ever asked me whether my people can suffer well. Nobody has asked me whether they are holy, whether their marriages tell the truth, whether they could stand in front of Pilate, whether a single one of them fears the LORD. There is no line on any denominational report for that, and I understand why, you cannot count it. But a pastor measured by crowd size will, given enough Mondays, preach the god who draws crowds. The nice god draws crowds. That is not a theory, it is arithmetic I have lived, and here is the sentence I have needed thirty chapters of my life to say plainly. The nice god fills rooms, and I filled rooms with him, and I stood in the lobby afterward and received thanks for it, and there is applause down that road all the way to the last mile.

Let me show you the inventory, because confession that stays general is just mood. I went back through years of my own sermons, the same audit I described in the second chapter, and catalogued what had quietly gone missing. Wrath survived, but always with a hedge around it, always immediately domesticated by three qualifications before anyone could flinch. Hell went nearly silent, and when it did appear it arrived with an apology attached, the doctrinal equivalent of a cough. Repentance softened into growth, an invitation to become rather than a summons to turn. And sin, this is the one that grieves me most, sin became brokenness, and I want you to see what that substitution does, because I chose it consciously and I chose it often. Brokenness is something that happens to you. Sin is something you do. Brokenness needs healing, sin needs forgiveness, and only one of the two requires anyone to kneel. I put an entire congregation in the passive voice for years, and I did it because the passive voice does not require an apology to God, and no one ever sent a concerned email about being called broken. It is the perfect anesthetic. It sounds compassionate, it is half true, and it removes the one thing, guilt, that the gospel exists to deal with. A church full of broken people needs a therapist. A church full of sinners needs a Savior. I knew which one filled rooms.

Judgment I did keep preaching, and this is the part of the confession that costs the most, because I kept it by aiming it. It is astonishingly easy to preach a fierce god at people who are not in the room. The nationalist pulpit does it every week, thundering against the culture, the coasts, the universities, while the god presented to the congregation itself is a mascot, warm, proud of them, one of us. The progressive pulpit runs the identical liturgy at the other wall, thundering against the nationalists with magnificent courage while its own people bask, unindicted, in the glow of being the good ones. Both rooms hear a holy god and a nice god every single week, holiness for the enemy, niceness for the tribe, and both rooms leave feeling that ancient warmth of having been on the right side of a wrath pointed elsewhere. That is not the recovery of the fear of the LORD. That is arms dealing. And I have done my seasons of it, choosing prophetic targets my particular room would enjoy seeing hit, and collecting the courage discount, because it looks exactly like boldness and costs exactly nothing. Here is the test I now use on myself, and I offer it to every preacher and every congregation. Does the holy God ever turn, in your pulpit, and speak against you, your side, your base, the people whose giving keeps the lights on. If the fire only ever falls on the people who are not there, it is not the fire of God. It is stage lighting.

I founded a network that connects pastors, thousands of them now, and I need to testify to what I have heard there, because this chapter is not finally about me. I have sat with this confession in a hundred accents. The pastor who knows exactly what the text in front of him says and preaches something adjacent to it, and hates himself quietly in the car. The man carrying a building loan in one hand and Isaiah 6 in the other, doing the math no seminary prepared him for, where faithfulness and the mortgage point different directions. The young preacher who watched a mentor say one true hard thing and get shredded for it, and learned the lesson the system was teaching. I want to say this with grief and not contempt, because contempt is the cheap version of this chapter. These men are not hirelings, not most of them. They are shepherds who were handed a job description written by a market, told the sheep are customers, measured on volume, and left alone with the arithmetic. The system disciplines them toward the nice god with the same patient feedback that disciplined me, and systems win against tired men, and the American church is staffed almost entirely by tired men. When a thousand pulpits all drift the same direction, the interesting question is not who is weak. It is who built the current.

But I cannot leave it on the system, because the system did not stand in my pulpit. I did. And the cost of my drift was not abstract, it was seated in the rows in front of me, and I told you about him two chapters ago. The man whose daughter died, whose warm small faith came apart at the graveside because it had never been given anything weight-bearing to stand on, had been sitting under preaching, some of it mine, for years before the cold came. I have had to ask myself the question that has no comfortable answer, and I will write it down rather than soften it. In all those years of pleasant, helpful, well-received sermons, what had I given him to stand on. I do not know. That is the honest answer. I know what I had given him a hundred chances to feel. I do not know what I had given him to hold, and a pastor who cannot answer that question about his own preaching has learned the most expensive thing this book has to teach, and he has learned it too late for at least one man, and that is a sentence I will carry to my own grave, and should.

What did repentance look like. Smaller and slower than the dramatic turn this chapter's shape wants, because real repentance always is. I named it to my congregation, not in these words but plainly, that I had fed them thinner bread than I was given, and that it would change. I started preaching the woe before the coal, the unmaking before the sending, sin in the active voice, judgment with our own name inside the blast radius, hell without the cough. And I will not pretend the story ends in revival, because this book does not tell that kind of lie. Some people left. Attendance, the old god, wobbled, and I felt the wobble in the exact organ where I used to feel the applause, which is how I learned the idol was still installed. But something else began happening in that room, harder to count and impossible to fake. People began confessing things out loud, to God and to each other, real things. The prayers after the service got longer and quieter. And more than once, a person found me at the door, the place where they used to say nice sermon, and said instead, with something in their face I had not seen before, I felt like God was actually in there today. He had been there the whole time, of course. It was never the room he had left. It was the preaching, and the preaching was never the room's decision. It was mine. Many turned back at Capernaum too, after the sermon Jesus refused to soften, and he watched them go, and asked the twelve if they wanted to leave as well, and did not chase the crowd down the road with a survey. I spent years of my ministry chasing that crowd. I am not finished repenting of it. But I have at least stopped calling the chase a calling, and I have stopped reading the full room as the smile of God, because I know now what the fullness cost, and who paid it, and the rooms were full. That was the problem.
chapters.verdict: The rooms were full. That was the problem.
reflect: Bell describes being trained by his congregation's feedback one degree at a time. Where has approval quietly trained you away from something you believe?
In your church's preaching, does the holy God ever turn and speak against your own side, or does the fire only fall on people who are not in the room?
What is the difference between calling a congregation broken and calling it sinful, and which one have you been more often offered? Which did you prefer, and why?
If you measure a church by what it counts, what does your community actually worship? What would it look like to count what cannot be counted?

chapters.title: Living Under the God Who Is
chapters.summary: Revelation 1 unfolded. The disciple Jesus loved falls at his feet as though dead, and the majesty itself reaches down. From that island Bell walks into the three places the recovery happens, worship that expects the living God, prayer that reverses Samuel's sentence back to its right order, and the strange holiness of lives that make God seem likely. No bow at the end. The ground was always holy.
chapters.body:
If this book has done its work, you are standing in cleared ground. The nice god is dead, or dying, and the mean god was never anything but his shadow, and the question that remains is the practical one, the Tuesday question. How does a person actually live under the God who is. I am not going to answer it with a program, because a program is just the therapeutic reflex in work clothes, five steps to a manageable deity. What I can do is show you one more scene, the last great theophany in the Bible, because everything I know about living under the holy God is inside it, and then walk out from it into the three places where the recovery actually happens, the worship, the praying, and the life.

The scene is on Patmos, a penal island in the Aegean, near the end of the first century. An old man is there, exiled for the word of God, and the old man is John, and we need to remember exactly who John is before we watch what happens to him. This is not a stranger to Jesus. This is the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned back against his chest at the last supper, close enough to ask him a whispered question. He stood at the cross when the others ran. He ran to the empty tomb and saw the grave clothes folded. He has spent six decades preaching Christ, and he has earned, if any human being has ever earned it, the right to a warm reunion. On the Lord's day he hears behind him a voice like a trumpet, and he turns, and he sees one like a son of man, standing among seven golden lampstands, clothed in a long robe, the hairs of his head white, like white wool, like snow, and his eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet like burnished bronze refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. From his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength. It is Jesus. It is his oldest living friend on earth, and John tells us exactly what the reunion did to him. When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead.

Do not let the familiarity of Scripture flatten that. The apostle of love, the man who wrote God is love, the man who had touched him, eaten with him, leaned on him, drops like a corpse at his feet. Sixty years of intimacy did not make Jesus manageable. Whatever the risen Christ is now, in glory, he is not smaller than he was at the supper, and the man who knew his heartbeat cannot stand up in front of him. If John fell as though dead, then the casualness we have cultivated, the buddy Christ, the boyfriend of the worship chorus, the affirming presence of ten thousand sermons, is not intimacy. It is distance wearing intimacy's clothes, the certain mark of people describing someone they have never seen. And then comes the gesture the whole Bible has been building toward, and I want it to land with its full weight. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.

The hand. The same hand that touched the leper, laid on a man lying as dead. The First and the Last stoops, and the fear not he speaks is not the greeting-card version, because look at what he grounds it in. Not, fear not, I would never hurt you. Fear not, I died, and I am alive forever, and I hold the keys of Death and Hades. It is the most terrifying resume in existence, offered as the comfort. This is everything this book has been trying to say, compressed into one gesture on one island. The holy God does not comfort us by being small. He comforts us by being unimaginably large and turned toward us. John is not raised from the floor by a reduction in Christ's majesty. He is raised by the majesty itself, reaching down. Unmade at his feet, raised by his hand, and the order never reverses, in Scripture or in a life. Nobody is raised who was not first down. Every counterfeit god in this book is an attempt to get the hand without the floor, the fear not without the falling, and it cannot be done, and the whole Christian life is learning to stop trying.

So, worship. Begin there, because Sunday is where the recovery starts or fails. The writer Annie Dillard, in 1982, looked at the mild proceedings of American churches and asked whether any of us actually believed a word of what we were saying, because if we did, she wrote, we would come to services wearing crash helmets, and the ushers would lash us to the pews, since the sleeping God we so casually invoke may one day wake and take offense. She was not being whimsical. She was reading Exodus. And I want to be careful about what trembling worship is not, because the aesthetic is fakeable and the fake is its own disease. It is not gloom, not organ music versus guitars, not manufactured solemnity, not volume in either direction. I have felt the fear of the LORD in a plain room with bad carpet and out-of-tune singing, and I have felt its total absence in cathedrals. Trembling worship is a matter of expectation. It is a room full of people who have come on the working assumption that the living God may actually be present, that the one who fills the room outranks everyone in it, that something could happen here that no one on the platform can control. You cannot program that. But you can stop programming against it, which is what we mostly do now, every silence filled, every transition smoothed, every possible surprise rehearsed out, a liturgy of risk management. Hebrews, the same letter that gave us the surgeon, ends its great chapter by telling us we have received a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and therefore, it says, let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire. That last line is present tense, new covenant, this side of the cross. The fire did not retire at Calvary. It became approachable. Those are different words.

Then prayer, and here the recovery is quieter and harder. Prayer to the nice god is a monologue with a warm echo, and I say that as a man who has spent whole seasons doing it, presenting my slate of requests to my own kindest voice and calling the mild afterglow an answer. Prayer under the God who is has a different grammar in every mood. Petition becomes daring again, because it is addressed to someone free, someone who might say no, someone whose no to me has been, more times than I can count, the only thing that saved me. Confession becomes specific, sins with names, said aloud, in the active voice, because I am not informing him of anything, I am agreeing with him at last, and agreement is where the lightness comes from. And listening returns, the discipline the therapeutic age has almost erased, because a god who is your own reflection has nothing to tell you that you do not already think. The boy Samuel was taught one sentence to pray, speak, for your servant hears, and I have come to believe it is the whole curriculum. Most of my praying life I have prayed its exact inverse, listen, for your servant speaks. The reversal of those two words is the reversal of everything, and it takes years, and silence, and it is worth it, because the God who is actually speaks, through the word mostly, in ways that redirect actual Tuesdays, and the man who has once heard him will never again be content with the echo.

Then holiness, the life itself, and let me clear the word before I commend it, because the word has been ruined twice. Holiness does not mean the scrubbed respectability of the suburban church, the not-drinking, not-cursing, lawn-mowed moralism that the word evokes for a generation of the burned. That is the mean god's residue. And it does not mean intensity of religious feeling either. Holiness means otherness that has moved in, the fire of the bush becoming, slowly, the temperature of an ordinary human life. He disciplines us, Hebrews said, that we may share his holiness. Be holy, for I am holy, is how Peter puts it, quoting Leviticus across fifteen centuries. What it looks like, in a therapeutic age, is a strangeness the age has no shelf for. People who tell the truth when a lie would be cheaper. People who keep vows through the years when the vows cost the most. People who confess their sins out loud, first and specifically, before anyone else's. People who are unanxious about the things the whole world is anxious about, and grieved by things the world cannot see at all. People who can sit with the dying without chatter, because they know the one holding the keys. I have met perhaps a few dozen such people in fifteen years of ministry, and every one of them had the same effect on a room. They made God seem likely. No apologetic argument I have ever deployed has done for a skeptic what ten minutes with one of those lives does, and I say that as a man argument brought a long way. The recovery of the holy God will not finally be preached into the American church. It will be lived into it, by the strange ones, the way it always has been.

C.S. Lewis, in the notebook he kept after his wife died, published in 1961 as A Grief Observed, wrote that his idea of God was not a divine idea, that it had to be shattered time after time, and that the shattering was one of the marks of God's presence, because the living God is himself the great iconoclast, breaking every image we make of him, including the devout ones. I have found that to be the most reliable single test in the spiritual life. The god who never surprises you, never contradicts you, never breaks the frame you built for him, is the god you made, however orthodox his features. The living God breaks your images of him, and the breaking is a kindness, the way it would be a kindness to smash a portrait a man had begun mistaking for his wife. I have had my god broken more times than I can now count, at my conversion, in the hard years of the pastorate, at gravesides, in the faces of my sons, and every breaking felt like loss and every one was rescue. That is how you know him, in the end. The idol holds still. He does not.

So we end where I promised we would not end, without a bow. I am not going to tell you that the holy God will make your life go well. That was the other god's pitch, and you know now what his promises were worth. I am telling you what John learned on the island, what Isaiah learned in the smoke, what a fatherless atheist learned in the wreck of his certainties and has spent fifteen years of ministry watching hold when nothing else held. The God who is will not fit in your palm. He will not stay outside the shell. He will unmake you before he sends you, cut you where you needed cutting, break every small picture you paint of him, and cost you the life you had planned. And he will lay his right hand on you, the one holding the keys of death, and he will say fear not, and he will be the only one in the universe entitled to say it. He was never nice. He was never safe. He is holy, and he is good, and he has been standing in the fire at the edge of your ordinary Tuesday for a long time now, waiting for you to turn aside. The ground you are standing on is holy ground. It always was. Take off your shoes.
chapters.verdict: He was never nice. He is good, and he is God.
reflect: John knew Jesus more intimately than any man alive and still fell as though dead. What does our casualness with Christ suggest about whom we are actually addressing?
The risen Jesus grounds fear not in the most terrifying resume in existence. Why is a comfort built on majesty stronger than a comfort built on smallness?
Most of us pray, listen, for your servant speaks. What would it cost you to reverse those words, and what might it return?
Lewis called God the great iconoclast. What image of God has been broken in your life, and looking back, was the breaking loss or rescue?
